title: Seeking workflow experiences
author: flavorfox
selftext:
I'd love to hear peoples workflows and prompt styles. I'm not so interested in the one-shotted prompts, but how people are working with AI with purpose and direction.

I've personally experienced and kind of failed to use AI generated assets in my 2D retro style game (the generated assets are very far from ready to use, in terms of style, resolution, palette, animation etc.)

How are you working with it? How big tasks do you work on, how do you direct it, how do you work with it when it doesn't do as expected? Have you built tools with AI that help your workflow?

comments.author: United-Tour5043
comments.body:
its not prompts. its specs. you should create the game before asking the ai to create a spec. then use the spec for the ai to build from it. test every feature (either you test or ask for an ai to score on X/Y/Z metrics). 

do not believe the 1-shot prompts. they are 5k lines specs not prompts.

replies.author: flavorfox
replies.body:
But how do you go from the initial spec to bug fixing and iterations on things that needs to be changed, or where the requirements have changed since the original spec.

Even with a thourough spec i imagine even a small game will have 100s of items that are incorrect or needs adjustment or expansion.

replies.author: Binary-Trees
replies.body:
Make sure your project has clear documents on what you want to do, and what needs updated and changed. Update these documents as you go. I use godot, vs code, codex, pixelorama and github currently

Each time I do a change I have it write me a github update detailing changes, then I move those from the road map/updates document to the archived changes document.

comments.author: Professor_Snipe
comments.body:
I came to making my game (turn based, mechanics-heavy grindy RPG with 3x3 vs 3x3 combat) with a very detailed combat design I had from my previous attempt at making the game without AI. Basically I have a rulebook in several CSVs that I wrote that needed implementing, which regulates how everything should work together. That was the skeleton of all the mechanics, all of which I fed to Opus 5.5 on high reasoning. Claude.md specified that every uncertainty needed to be consulted and resolved with me. I answered ca. 100 questions then.

What I failed to do in 2 months Claude did in ONE freaking hour. All mechanics were in, all calculations were proper, the fairly intricate network of skill/trait/passive interactions was in and working absolutely perfectly. All with placeholder assets across the board, but it was just working.

Everything is in, every system works like I imagined, to the letter. I'm at the stage of preparing progression, implementing assets, creating enemies and playable characters as well as balancing itemisation. Then comes the adventure which I also have already written. It's incredible. I was very anti-AI before, but doing something like this first-hand has really opened my eyes on things.

replies.author: flavorfox
replies.body:
After working a lot on the workflow for the last few hours, I think my main problem is this:

My assets are 16x16 and image generation just isn't great at doing this resolution. I can get pretty great assets at sizes like 96x96 and probably smaller, but at 16x16 where every pixel matter i just can't get it right. It either spirals into noisy pixel soup, or super simplistic sprites that looks like placeholder art.

I've tried various variations of generating concept art first, using template art, having it not simply scaling it by recreating it in 16x16, etc.

I've tried working with claude, chatgpt, pixellab etc and none of them comes even close to being usable - at least not for generating straight from prompt->finished asset.

comments.author: Zenity07
comments.body:
I use AI how I would use a development team. Where I know exactly what I want, I will give very specific instructions. Where I am not so sure, I ask for input first. A lot of it is trial and error. Managing AI effectively is really not so different from managing people in this regard.

The biggest AI superpower IMO is in building custom tools that let you and the AI build things faster. More effective design tools, more effective ways to verify results, more effective ways to procedurally generate content, etc.

I particularly like to build tools that let me communicate more effectively with the AI, like marking specific places directly in game. If there's an area where I find the AI can't do a good enough job yet, then I think instead about how I can build tools that allow me to do it faster myself.

One thing that also often gets overlooked is that you rarely develop anything in a vacuum. Anything you have build before is something the AI can reference and build on. Over time things get easier, and you can get a lot of value from maintaining a shared knowledge base between different projects. Where no reference exists, you can create one, e.g. start by cloning an existing project as a reference, then iterate on it until it feels right and let the AI keep notes of what you learned in the process. Then apply these lessons to your actual project.

comments.author: orellanaed
comments.body: On a retro 2D game the generated sprite is never palette-ready so lock the hex colors and the cell size in the prompt and fix the sheet by hand before it goes in SpriteFrames.

comments.author: SirStarshine
comments.body: I'm working on a gardening game in Unity, and I'm using a combination of ChatGPT, Claude and Aura. I fleshed out the idea with GPT as well as been coming up with images for plants. I mainly use Aura for direct Unity development, though I've also used Claude briefly for this. Claude is mainly for coding, and even developed a personal utility for animating the still images.

comments.author: No-Marketing-9238
comments.body:
The biggest thing i learned as a vibe coder is that AI can build and implement the tools into the game to help me make things work how i want.  Two examples:

I was building an Auralux style RTS (Prismatic Dominion on the app store, check it out!) and I couldnt get the AI enemies to remain competitive with human players.  

AI build an AI logic debugger that could export every decision the AI made and why during a game, then claude could analyze that and find where the issues where.

The 2nd example is in an Inflation style RPG, a 2D top down game.  The walking paths, asset placements, doors, and bosses wherent being placed exactly where i wanted them.  So it built me an in game debugger with authoring tools, so that while i am playing the game, i can pull out the debugger and manually change things that arent working

  
1 more example just for fun.  My company uses wordpress for our learning and development.  We didnt have a great free way to import storyline courses into it, or tracking SCORM, without a paid plugin.  ChatGPT build a free plugin that does both, excellently, and it took maybe 15 minutes
